## Study title

Engaging the Immune System to Kill Solid Tumors in Pet Dogs - A Comparative Oncology Approach (TriKE + Radiation Therapy)

## Purpose of study

The purpose of the study is to identify a safe and effective dose of a novel immunotherapy drug (TriKE) when given with hypofractionated radiation therapy (RT) in companion dogs with a sarcoma. 

## Eligibility criteria

Dogs must: 

  * Have cytologically or histopathologicaly confirmed sarcoma, measuring at least 2cm
  * Weigh at least 7 kg (15 lbs)
  * Modified performance score less than 2 and expected survival of at least 2 months

# Open Clinical Trials

The Comparative Oncology Program (COP) designs and implements clinical trials in collaboration with academic veterinary institutions across the United States. Pet animals will receive treatment under the care of board-certified veterinary oncologists who share our goal of alleviating the suffering of companion animals with cancer. Information gained by the clinical trials will be used to benefit both animals and humans with cancer.

### COTC029: Pilot assessment of BG34-200 in spontaneous canine cancers

The purpose of this study is to evaluate dose escalation of BG34-200 in dogs with cancer. We will 1) evaluate the safety of BG34-200, and 2) evaluate the ability of BG34-200 to stimulate a patient’s immune system to detect and destroy cancer cells.

Learn More

### COTC033: Repurposing vaccine immunity to treat cancers: validation in canine patients

This clinical trial, led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI), in collaboration with Dr. John T. Schiller, assesses the safety and effectiveness of intra-tumoral administered vaccines, when given to dogs with cancer.

# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. Families may still be responsible for additional veterinary expenses, travel, lodging, and repeated visits over several weeks or months, especially when a study is located far from home.

The following links are intended to help pet parents and veterinary professionals find information about current canine oncology trials being conducted throughout the United States and, in some cases, internationally.

We encourage families to carefully review each study’s eligibility requirements, location, potential costs, time commitment, and possible benefits and risks with their veterinary team.

## Start Here: Nationwide Search Tools

If you are not sure where to begin, start with the AVMA registry. It lets you search by cancer type and by location, which is faster than checking individual centers one at a time.

#### AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

The AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, formerly known as the AVMA Animal Health Studies Database, helps dog parents and veterinary professionals find veterinary clinical studies taking place throughout the United States and Canada. By making this information easier to access, the registry supports continued research and progress in veterinary medicine and canine health care.

If you are interested in a clinical trial for your dog, begin by discussing the study and your dog’s potential eligibility with your veterinary care provider.

 

AVMA Clinical Trials

#### National Cancer Institute, Comparative Oncology Program

The Comparative Oncology Program develops and conducts clinical trials in partnership with veterinary teaching institutions throughout the United States. Dogs enrolled in these studies receive care from board-certified veterinary oncologists committed to improving comfort, quality of life, and cancer care for companion animals.

The knowledge gained through this research may help advance the understanding of cancer and support future progress in both canine and human oncology.

National Cancer Institute

#### PetCure Oncology

PetCure Oncology provides stereotactic radiation surgery and stereotactic radiation therapy, commonly known as SRS and SRT. These highly precise forms of radiation therapy have been used in human oncology and are now available for dogs with certain types of cancer.

PetCure Oncology reports using SRS and SRT in thousands of companion animals with a variety of tumor types. Its affiliated veterinary specialists continue to study these approaches to better understand their potential benefits, safety considerations, side effects, and appropriate applications in canine cancer care.

PetCure Oncology Clinical Trials

#### ACI Biosciences

Network conducting trials at participating private practices.

ACI Biosciences Clinical Trials

## Keep in Mind

Clinical trials may explore new approaches to diagnosing or supporting dogs with cancer. These may include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical procedures, temperature-based therapies, immunotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and other emerging approaches.

Although many clinical trials take place at veterinary colleges and teaching hospitals, a growing number of specialty and referral practices also participate in canine cancer research. Some studies require every appointment to be completed at the participating institution, while others may allow certain tests, procedures, or follow-up visits to be handled by a dog’s regular veterinary team.

The words “experimental” and “investigational” can understandably feel concerning. Before a new therapy or procedure reaches a veterinary clinical trial, researchers have typically completed earlier stages of evaluation. However, unknowns may remain regarding its safety, effectiveness, or potential side effects. A study is offered because researchers believe the approach may provide meaningful benefits, but participation does not guarantee a positive outcome.

Pet parents should review the study’s purpose, requirements, possible benefits, known and unknown risks, costs, and available alternatives with the clinical trial team and their dog’s veterinary care provider before making a decision.

# Open veterinary clinical trials are currently recruiting

The Cornell University Hospital for Animals is actively engaged in clinical studies that work towards applicable treatments and cures for our patients. Please consider informing owners of eligible patients about relevant studies, and help us move the research forward!

#### Featured Trial:  Pain treatment for canine cancer patients

  * BACKGROUND: Some dogs with cancer, especially end-stage cancer patients or patients with dermatitis secondary to radiation therapy, experience pain that cannot be adequately controlled with oral medications given by their owners at home. Depending on the site of pain, an epidural injection can provide pain relief superior to oral medications, sometimes with fewer side effects. The duration of pain relief is variable but may last several weeks. Repeating the injection requires heavy sedation or general anesthesia each time, and this puts the dog at risk for anesthetic complications, is time consuming, and can be prohibitively expensive.

# Canine T-cell Lymphoma Trial

## Biodynamic Testing of Chemotherapy Sensitivity in Dogs Receiving Gemcitabine for Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma

### Principal Investigator

Dr. Michael Childress, Professor of Comparative Oncology

### Background

Epitheliotropic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (ETCL) in dogs is a skin cancer for which few effective therapies exist. The chemotherapy drug gemcitabine is commonly used to treat humans with this cancer. Although gemcitabine has been shown to be well-tolerated in dogs, its use as a treatment for dogs with ETCL has not been described.

In this clinical trial, we will enroll 10 dogs with ETCL to test the efficacy of gemcitabine against this cancer. In addition, we will test the ability of a novel tissue imaging technology, biodynamic imaging (BDI), to predict the responsiveness of ETCL to gemcitabine.

We have shown in previous studies BDI predicts the response of primary nodal lymphomas in dogs to chemotherapy with approximately 80-90% accuracy. This will be the first time that BDI is used to predict the response of canine ETCL to a chemotherapy drug.

# Veterinary Clinical Trials

Clinical trials at VROC help evaluate new cancer treatments for pets by assessing their safety, effectiveness, and potential side effects. Participation is entirely voluntary, and the decision to enroll your pet is yours. However, enrollment in a clinical trial is required for a patient to be seen in our clinic.

Our studies build upon the current standard of care using the same advanced technologies available in leading specialty pet cancer hospitals. While specific outcomes cannot be guaranteed, our team is committed to providing the highest standard of veterinary oncology care throughout each trial.

For questions or to learn more about available studies, please contact Paige Neumann, Research Study Coordinator, at 214-645-6221 or by VROC@UTSouthwestern.edu (no-reply@utsouthwestern.edu).

### Other clinical trials

Visit the University of Minnesota’s Clinical Investigation Center, for current enrollment information for all pet animal clinical trials.

### About clinical trials

Clinical trials, or clinical studies, take place in the clinic, a step after lab research studies. They offer experimental treatments to patients who fit the criteria of a particular study and are used to determine whether new drugs or treatments are both safe and effective.

There is some risk with any clinical trial, just as with many medical procedures; however, all clinical trials are reviewed by an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) before they can begin. Also, informed owner consent is always part of clinical trials, so before your pet enters a study you will be given all information up front and must agree in writing. In many clinical trials, patients must be treated at the clinic conducting the trial and may not receive study drugs remotely.

Research ethics at the University of Minnesota. We are committed to protecting research participants, upholding ethical standards, and improving our practice at every step of our work.

# SBRT for Canine Lung Tumor Study

  * Recruiting
  * Dog
  * Oncology

Primary pulmonary carcinomas in dogs are most commonly treated with surgery, which can result in survival times of approximately one year. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) is a highly precise form of radiation therapy that delivers high doses of radiation directly to a tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding normal tissues. The purpose of this study is to evaluate dogs with primary pulmonary carcinoma treated using a standardized SBRT protocol across institutions participating in the Veterinary Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (VRTOG).

## Inclusion Criteria

Dogs are eligible for enrollment if they meet all of the following criteria:

  * Cytologic or histopathologic diagnosis of a single primary pulmonary carcinoma.
  * Primary lung tumor measuring greater than 1 cm in its shortest diameter.
  * No previous treatment for the lung tumor.
  * No diagnosis of another malignant tumor outside the lungs within 30 days before enrollment.

# Clinical Trial Development

## Synopsis of the NCI Comparative Oncology Trial Consortium

Image: two people with a pet dog

The Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium (COTC) is an active network of nineteen academic comparative oncology centers, centrally managed by the NIH-NCI-Center for Cancer Research's Comparative Oncology Program, that functions to design and execute clinical trials in dogs with cancer to assess novel therapies. The goal of this effort is to answer biological questions geared to inform the development path of these agents for future use in human cancer patients. Trials conducted by the COTC are pharmacokinetically and pharmacodynamically rich with the product of this work directly integrated into the design of current human Phase I and II clinical trials. Our trials are carried at COTC member institutions, which currently include 19 sites. See examples of published COTC trials.

## How We Operate

Image: Children petting a dog

The NCI and COTC members sign a Memorandum of Understanding every 4 years to allow NCI to take the lead on dealings with all companies/institutions which have a desire to interact with the COTC.

# Mammary Carcinoma, Squamous Cell Carcinoma, AGASACA, and Melanoma Clinical Trial

## Benefits and Participation 

  * Owners are financially responsible for the initial exam and screening tests to determine eligibility. 
  * Following the initial exam and screening, the remainder of this trial is funded for up to 2 months of treatment including tumor biopsy, recheck exams, bloodwork, and chemotherapy. 
  * Recheck visits for blood draws and monitoring are required and covered by the study. 

## Inclusion Criteria

  * Diagnosis of mammary carcinoma, melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, histiocytic sarcoma, or apocrine anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA)
  * Measurable tumor on physical exam 
  * Prior cancer treatment is allowed, but dogs must have cancer progression at the time of enrollment 
  * Pet must be otherwise healthy

## Clinical Trial Background

  * Cancer is ranked as the top cause of death in dogs. 
  * New anti-cancer therapies are desperately needed. 
  * Palbociclib is an oral chemotherapy drug used in various human cancers. 
  * Palbociclib has the potential to treat many canine cancers, however, the ideal dose has yet to be established in dogs. 

## Contact

Please direct any questions regarding the enrollment of a patient to the Auburn Oncology Service.

# Cancer Clinical Studies/Trials

## Cancer

## Image: Cancer Clinical Studies/TrialsCancer Clinical Studies/Trials

The CCAH works with the school's Veterinary Center for Clinical Trials to manage oncology trials for cancer studies in cats, dogs and horses, with the goal of creating better, more-effective treatments for patients. Current and recently completed cancer studies include:

### Orally administered rapamycin in dogs with cancer

The drug rapamycin is currently approved for immunosuppression during preparatory and maintenance regimens for organ and bone marrow transplant in human patients. Our study evaluates the safety and effectiveness of rapamycin when given orally to dogs with cancer.

### Thermal ablation of cancer in dogs and cats

Our study evaluates the outcome of treating dogs and cats with minimally invasive tumor ablation technologies, including cryoablation and microwave ablation. These methods are used to treat cancers in people, but information in animals is very limited.
